records.table: Near Kyoto stands Yamazaki, Japan's first malt whisky distillery, founded in 1923, and The Yamazaki 12 Years Old is Suntory's single malt from it, married from American oak, sherry and Mizunara casks. Peach, candied orange and vanilla give way to a long, spiced finish.
records.story: Shinjiro Torii (1879 to 1962), whose Osaka company grew into Suntory, resolved to make a whisky for Japanese drinkers, and in 1923 began building a distillery at Yamazaki, between Osaka and Kyoto, where the Katsura, Uji and Kizu rivers meet and the damp air suits maturing whisky. Masataka Taketsuru (1894 to 1979), back from his studies in Scotland, worked on Yamazaki before he left to found Yoichi in 1934. The distillery's first whisky, Shirofuda, followed in 1929, and for decades Yamazaki's malt found its way into Suntory's blends. Torii's second son, Keizo Saji (1919 to 1999), became the company's second president in 1961 and its second master blender. In 1984 he brought out Yamazaki as a single malt, when Japanese drinkers mostly chose blends; the bottle was labelled at first as a pure malt, and in 2004 the twelve year old's label took the words single malt. Because Japanese houses seldom trade spirit, Yamazaki makes its own range of characters from pot stills of many shapes and casks of three woods. Fruit, oak and spice held in balance: the 12 is what Japanese single malt means in a glass.

records.table: Suntory built Hakushu in 1973 in forest on the slopes of Mount Kaikoma in Yamanashi, and The Hakushu 12 Years Old is its lightly peated single malt. Green apple, pear and mint sit over a thin thread of smoke, and long with soda it makes a cool highball.
records.story: Suntory made its malt at Yamazaki alone for half a century. Keizo Saji (1919 to 1999), the founder's son and the company's second president from 1961, led the building of a second malt distillery, and Hakushu was founded in 1973, fifty years after Yamazaki. It stands in forest on the slopes of Mount Kaikoma, in the Southern Alps of Yamanashi Prefecture, and the house calls it the forest distillery. Its water is groundwater that, by Suntory's account, has run through the granite of the mountains behind it and comes out soft. A second distillery gave Suntory's blenders a second character, and Hibiki joins Hakushu malt with Yamazaki's and with grain whisky. Under the Hakushu name the single malt shows that character alone, green and lightly smoked. In 2018 Suntory paused sales of the 12 in Japan, because too little whisky of that age stood in its warehouses, and brought it back in 2021. Herbs, orchard fruit and only a whisper of peat make the Hakushu 12 the counterweight to the Yamazaki, a malt that suits a highball as well as a glass poured neat.

records.table: Direct coal fire heats the pot stills that make Nikka Single Malt Yoichi, at the distillery Masataka Taketsuru built on the Hokkaido coast in 1934. Ripe fruit and oak come first, then firm peat with a roasted edge, and sweet smoke to finish.
records.story: Masataka Taketsuru (1894 to 1979), the son of a sake-brewing family from Takehara, went to Glasgow in 1918 to learn how Scotch whisky was made, and in 1920 married Rita Cowan (1896 to 1961) there. Back in Japan he worked on Yamazaki, then left to build a distillery of his own. He chose Yoichi, on the Hokkaido coast, for a cold, damp climate he thought close to Scotland's, and in 1934 founded Dai Nippon Kaju there, a company that made apple juice while its first spirit aged; Nikka is drawn from the words Nippon Kaju. Its first whisky came out in 1940. Yoichi kept the direct coal firing of its pot stills that Taketsuru had learnt in Scotland, a method rare in distilleries because the fire is hard to control. In 2015 Nikka withdrew its age-statement Yoichi malts, and the no-age-statement Single Malt Yoichi took their place. Ten of the distillery's buildings stand on Japan's list of Important Cultural Properties. Heavier and smoky, Yoichi belongs beside a Suntory single malt: together the two span how far one country's whisky can range.

records.table: Where two rivers meet near Sendai, Nikka built its second distillery in 1969, and Nikka Single Malt Miyagikyo is its soft, fruity malt. Steam-heated stills give apple, pear and vanilla: pour it as a gentle foil to the coal-fired smoke of Yoichi.
records.story: Three decades of malt at Yoichi on Hokkaido lay behind Masataka Taketsuru (1894 to 1979) by the 1960s, and by Nikka's account he wanted a second malt of another character, so that blending different malts could give a more complex whisky. He found his site near Sendai, in Miyagi Prefecture, between the Hirose and Nikkawa rivers. The story goes that he tasted the river water, diluted a whisky with it, and settled on the place. The distillery opened in 1969, first called the Sendai distillery. Where Yoichi fires its pot stills with coal, Miyagikyo heats its stills gently with indirect steam, and its spirit comes off softer and fruitier. Nikka's Coffey stills, brought from Scotland in 1963 and first set up at Nishinomiya, were moved to Miyagikyo in 1999, to make the grain whisky for the house's blends. When Nikka withdrew its age-statement Miyagikyo malts in 2015, Single Malt Miyagikyo, with no age statement, took over the label. Yoichi is its partner: pour the two side by side, and a guest tastes how the shape and heat of a still change a malt.

records.table: At the foot of Kiso Komagatake, 798 metres up in Nagano, Hombo Shuzo distils Mars Single Malt Komagatake, its core single malt. Married from bourbon barrels and casks that held sherry, port and wine, it gives apple tea, apricot and ripe persimmon.
records.story: Mars whisky began in 1949, when Hombo Shuzo, a drinks house of Kagoshima in the south of Japan, took up whisky under the guidance of the man who had been Masataka Taketsuru's superior at Settsu Shuzo in Osaka and had sent him to Scotland. The story goes that this man drew on the report Taketsuru wrote of his Scottish studies when he planned Hombo's stills. In 1960 Hombo opened a works in Yamanashi, and in 1985 its whisky equipment was moved from there to Miyada in Nagano, where the Mars Shinshu Distillery was founded, 798 metres up at the foot of Kiso Komagatake. Distilling stopped in 1992, and the stills stood silent for nineteen years before malt distilling began again in 2011. In 2024 the distillery took the name Mars Komagatake, and in 2025 Hombo Shuzo made Single Malt Komagatake, until then a yearly release, a core bottling at 45% ABV. Neither Suntory nor Nikka makes it, and that is its lesson: a mountain malt showing that Japanese single malt reaches further than the two large firms.
